Title: Effect of Laser Remelting Power on the Microstructure and Tribological Properties of TiNbMo Medium-entropy Alloy Coatings; [激光重熔功率对 TiNbMo 中熵合金涂层微观结构 及摩擦学性能的影响 *]
Abstract: Owing to their high hardness, high-temperature structural stability, and wear resistance, laser cladding of refractory medium-and high-entropy alloy coatings has become a new research hotspot in the surface strengthening and protection of aerospace components. However, the single body-centered cubic structure of refractory medium-and high-entropy alloy coatings results in relatively low toughness and high friction coefficients, which, to some extent, limit their application on the surfaces of friction pairs. Currently, to simultaneously enhance the strength and toughness of refractory medium-and high-entropy alloys, researchers are attempting to enhance the grain size or phase distribution of materials through the design of alloy composition and structure optimization. Among these, lattice distortion strengthening, which can enhance the mechanical properties of a material without altering its crystal structure, has received extensive attention in the design of alloy compositions. In this study, three elements, Ti, Nb, and Mo were selected and mixed in an equal molar ratio as the basic component. A TiNbMo-refractory medium-entropy alloy coating was fabricated using laser-cladding technology. Ti has a hexagonal close-packed structure with dense packing and fewer slip planes and is prone to cylindrical slip, which is beneficial for enhancing the tribological properties of the coating. Two refractory metal elements, Nb and Mo, can be used as solid solution-strengthening elements to enhance the mechanical properties. Furthermore, to further reduce the cracks and unmelted particles in the coating, ensure a uniform phase distribution, enhance the toughness of the coating, and improve the anti-friction effect, the coating was subjected to a remelting treatment under a half-melting power of 1 kW and a melting power of 2 kW. This study systematically investigated the phase composition and interface characteristics, as well as the biphasic formation mechanism of a TiNbMo medium-entropy alloy coating. The influencing laws of laser remelting power on the hardness of the coating, as well as the friction and wear properties at room temperature and 600℃ were also studied. The results show that laser-clad TiNbMo medium-entropy alloy coatings are mainly composed of a solid-solution phase with a body-centered cubic structure and a dendritic phase with a Laves phase structure. After the remelting treatment, as the remelting power increases, the Laves phase content in the TiNbMo medium entropy alloy coating increases, degree of lattice distortion increases, and grain size becomes significantly finer. Owing to the significant lattice distortion, solid solution strengthening occurs, and a high cooling rate increases the grain boundary density, leading to grain boundary strengthening. Consequently, the microhardness of the remelted TiNbMo medium-entropy alloy coatings increases. The hardness values of the non-remelted coatings, 1 kW-remelted coatings and 2 kW-remelted coatings were 835.10, 815.10 and 864.25 HV0.3, respectively, which were approximately 2.30 to 2.40 times that of the microhardness of the substrate surface (363.08 HV0.3). The frictional properties of the coating were tested at both room temperature and 600℃. At room temperature, as the remelting power increased, the average friction coefficient of the coating decreased. The friction coefficient of the coating after 2 kW-remelting treatment was 0.45, which is 26% lower than that of the untreated coating. After remelting, the wear mechanism of the coating was mainly abrasive wear, accompanied by slight adhesive wear. At 600℃, the friction coefficient of the coating after 2 kW-remelting treatment was 0.52, which was approximately 30% lower than that of the untreated coating, and the wear rate of the coatings was 5.2×10−4 mm3 / (N·m). Compared with those of the unremelted coating (5.87×10−4 mm3 / (N·m)) and 1 kW-remelted coating (5.42×10−4 mm3 /( N·m)), it had a lower wear rate and exhibited superior friction-reducing and wear-resistant properties. This study analyzed the relationship between the phase composition and degree of lattice distortion of a medium-entropy alloy coating and its tribological properties. The influencing law of the laser remelting power on the mechanical properties of the medium-entropy alloy coating was obtained, which will provide theoretical support for the optimization design of high-performance medium-entropy alloy coatings. © 2026, Chinese Mechanical Engineering Society. Title: Spatially resolved phase transformation mapping in 410 stainless steel during additive manufacturing visualized via real-time infrared data
Abstract: In this study, we demonstrate that spatially resolved cooling curves derived from real-time infrared (IR) thermography during additive manufacturing (AM) can capture spatial variations in phase transformation temperatures through cooling curve analysis (CCA). Using this approach, we show that during laser hot-wire deposition of 410 stainless steel (410SS), the martensite start temperature (Ms) evolves dynamically throughout the build. The Ms temperature is spatially nonuniform, ranging from 185 ∘C to 348 ∘C, with the lowest values toward the build center and higher values toward the upper region of the deposit. In the lower portion of the build, no Ms inflection is detected via CCA, consistent with transformation occurring earlier during thermal cycling followed by tempering during subsequent thermal cycles. These trends in Ms are corroborated by characterizing the microstructure by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Traditionally, Ms is assumed to be constant, and a single interpass temperature is applied during both deposition and residual stress modeling. Our results demonstrate that IR-derived cooling curves provide a route to spatially and temporally resolved transformation temperature tracking for dynamic interpass control and improved residual-stress modeling. Title: High-throughput design of refractory multi principal element alloys for laser processing
Abstract: Refractory multi principal element alloys are promising for high temperature structural applications, but their high melting temperatures and segregation during bulk processing restrict conventional manufacturing routes. Laser-based melting or remelting enables localized high energy input and rapid cooling for these chemistries, yet crack-free processing remains a primary bottleneck. A key gap is the absence of screening workflows that explicitly target laser melting and validate predictions under relevant thermal conditions. Here, we implement staged screening plus validation framework that down-selects refractory ternary compositions and tests whether predicted solidification behavior remains compatible with laser remelting. A total of 3420 ternary compositions in the Hf–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr system, covering all twenty ternary subsystems, were screened by equilibrium CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) in TC-Python simulations for body-centered cubic (BCC) structure stability above 1000 °C, liquidus between 1680 °C and 2000 °C, and ΔT ≤ 50 °C to select six candidates, then ranked by Scheil Gulliver predictions and the Clyne crack susceptibility coefficient. Nb25Ti20Zr55 and Hf45Nb30Ti25 remained BCC dominated after arc melting and homogenization at 1350 °C for 1 h and successfully produced crack-free low porosity single track melt pools at 15.0 to 30.0 J mm−2. This framework links thermodynamic down selection to an operational crack-free remelt criterion. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Zhang X.; Zhang P.; Pu J.; Liao F.; Pang G.; Li F.; Hu X.; Bai Y.
Title: In situ self-layering bilayer alginate-gelatin hydrogels enabling synergistic adhesion and sensing for pressure distribution recognition
Abstract: Hydrogel-based wearable devices often struggle to integrate strong adhesion, long-term stability, and reliable sensing within a single system. Here, we present a one-step water–oil phase separation strategy that enables the in situ self-layering of bilayer hydrogels with robust interfacial coupling. The top poly(acrylamide-acrylic acid)-gelatin-alginate (poly(AM-AA)-gelatin-alginate) network provides mechanical resilience and environmental durability, while the bottom poly(butyl acrylate-2-hydroxyethyl acrylate)-glycerol-polycaprolactone methacrylic anhydride (poly(BA-HEA)-GPCL-MA) adhesive layer ensures strong yet reversible adhesion to diverse surfaces. This integrated architecture achieves a rare balance between adhesion, water retention stability, and sensing reliability, overcoming the long-standing trade-off in hydrogel-based electronics. Deformation-induced modulation of ionic conduction pathways endows the hydrogel with sensitive electromechanical sensing, enabling precise human-motion detection and Morse-code communication via controlled finger movements. As proof-of-concept, a 4 × 4 pressure-mapping array was integrated into robotic grippers, enabling tactile feedback to distinguish soft and rigid objects such as balloons and bottles. This work highlights a versatile design strategy for multifunctional hydrogels, paving new opportunities for smart interfaces, advanced human–machine interaction, and adaptive soft robotic systems. Title: Achieving exceptional strength-ductility synergy via strain disparity in an additively manufactured lamellar γ'-hardened medium-entropy alloy
Source title: Journal of Materials Science and Technology
Abstract: Precipitation-hardened medium/high-entropy alloys (M/HEAs) normally possess compromised strain hardening behavior concomitant with reduced ductility. Here, an exceptional strength-ductility synergy can be achieved in a novel laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) processed γ′-hardened lamellar sandwich structure, in which out-layer and inner-filling are ((CoCrNi)94Ti3Al3)98W2 and CoCrNi, respectively. After ageing at 700 °C for 1 h, the lamellar sandwich sample possesses a high ultimate tensile strength of 1293 MPa and a decent fractured strain of 33.2%. Electron microscopy characterizations show that γ′ precipitates within thermally stable cellular structures are detected in the outer-layer, and the broken-up cellular structures are observed within the inner-filling. Significantly, the strain concentration in the outer layer can be transferred to the inner filling with increasing tensile strain. An obvious strain disparity delays the critical strain concentration associated with failure, enabling the hard outer-layer to develop an enhanced dislocation multiplication and accommodation capacity by introducing dislocation pile-ups, stacking faults (SFs), Lomer-Cottrell locks (L-C locks), jog formation and deformation twins (DTs). The coordinated regulation of strain distribution via compositional and structural design thus provides a promising approach for preparing high-performance precipitation-strengthening metallic materials. © 2025

Title: Integration of additive manufacturing and coating technologies for aerospace components: performance, challenges, and future directions
Source title: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
Abstract: The aerospace industry has been a catalyst for the adoption of additive manufacturing (AM) and coating technologies to achieve superior performance (e.g., improved performance, lightweight structures, and increased durability). However, AM components fabricated directly through AM processes do not typically meet aerospace standards for surface characteristics, due to high surface roughness (Ra = 5–20 μm), residual porosity (0.1-2.0%), and tensile residual stress. This review examines the synergistic potential of combining AM and coating technologies to improve the performance of aerospace materials by investigating the relationships among structure, properties, and performance. The evaluation of AM-induced microstructural features and their impact on coating adhesion, thermal stability, and environmental resistance are discussed for four different methods of integrating AM and coatings: (1) Substrate tailoring through process parameter optimization, (2) Functionally graded material (FGM) interlayer development, (3) In-situ surface modifications during the AM process, and (4) Hybrid fabrication methods (combining traditional and advanced methods). Critical challenges identifying all four methods are explored. These include the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch between metallic substrates (12–18 × 10−6 °C−1) and ceramic coatings (8–11 × 10−6 °C−1). Other challenges are residual stress accumulation during the fabrication of AM components and the coating process, as well as degradation mechanisms that occur during AM, such as porosity-induced oxidation and columnar grain boundary diffusion. Lastly, a tiered roadmap for the industrial adoption of AM coatings is presented, along with emerging materials (high entropy alloys and nanocomposites) and self-healing properties. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The process optimization, wear and corrosion properties of WTaNbMo refractory high-entropy alloy coatings by laser cladding
Source title: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
Abstract: In this study, WTaNbMo refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) coatings were successfully fabricated on Inconel 718 substrate by laser cladding. Optimal coatings with superior comprehensive performances were systematically identified through orthogonal experimental design and Radar chart analysis. The phase composition, microstructural evolution, tribological behavior, and corrosion resistance of the RHEAs were comprehensively investigated, with emphasis on the effect of laser energy density ( L ed) on coating properties. The coatings predominantly consist of body-centered cubic (BCC), γ-(Ni, M) solid solutions, and Fe7(Nb, Ta)3 intermetallic compounds, attributed to high entropy effects and elemental diffusion. The results indicated that L ed significantly influenced the thermal behavior of molten pool, thereby regulating solidification rate, elemental distribution, microstructural uniformity, and defect formation. At an optimized L ed of 16.67 J/mm2, the coating exhibited a dense and homogeneous microstructure with reduced segregation and fewer defects, leading to a 304.45 % increase in microhardness compared with the substrate. The enhanced tribological performance was attributed to the synergistic effects of grain refinement, BCC solid-solution strengthening, improved coating densification, and enhanced deformation resistance, resulting in the lowest wear rate at room-temperature (RT). Electrochemical and immersion corrosion tests further demonstrated that the optimized L ed improved corrosion resistance, as evidenced by lower corrosion current density, higher charge-transfer resistance, and a 33.33 % reduction in corrosion rate compared with the substrate. This improvement was mainly related to the formation of a more compact coating structure and stable passive films that effectively inhibited Cl− penetration. © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: AlCoCrFeNi2. 1 eutectic high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on the surface of 35CrMo steel using four laser powers:1400, 1600,1800,and 2000 W. Title: High-Temperature Tribological Behavior of a Laser-Additively Manufactured CoCrNiFeAl-30 wt.% Cr3C2 Coating
Source title: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
Abstract: Dry sliding tests at 550, 750, and 950 °C were conducted to investigate the high-temperature tribological behavior of a laser-additively manufactured CoCrNiFeAl-30 wt.% Cr3C2 coating on 316L stainless steel. The coating exhibited a dense heterogeneous microstructure composed of FCC and BCC solid-solution phases together with Cr3C2 and Cr7C3 carbides. The friction coefficient changed only slightly with temperature, whereas the wear rate showed a non-monotonic variation, decreasing from 0.55 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 at 550 °C to 0.33 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 at 750 °C and then increasing to 1.16 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1 at 950 °C. SEM/EDS, XRD, and XPS analyses revealed progressively intensified tribo-oxidation with increasing temperature. However, the strongest oxidation at 950 °C did not produce the best wear resistance. Title: Recent Trends in Laser Cladding for Advanced Surface Engineering: A State-of-the-Art Review
Abstract: Laser cladding has emerged as a transformative surface engineering technology capable of depositing metallurgically bonded coatings with tailored microstructures and enhanced functional performance. This comprehensive review synthesizes to establish systematic correlations between laser processing parameters, melt-pool dynamics, solidification behavior, microstructural evolution, and the resultant mechanical, corrosion, and hydrogen embrittlement properties of clad coatings. The review critically examines how key parameters, namely, laser power, scanning speed, beam diameter, powder/wire feed rate, dilution, and overlap ratio, govern grain morphology, phase constitution, defect density, and residual stress states across Ni-based, Fe-based, Co-based, high-entropy alloy (HEA), and ceramic-reinforced composite systems. Optimized processing conditions consistently yield refined cellular or equiaxed microstructures with enhanced hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion performance. At the same time, excessive heat input promotes grain coarsening, dilution-induced phase destabilization, and increased defect susceptibility. Particular emphasis is placed on hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms in laser-clad layers, revealing a multiscale interplay between hydrogen diffusion, microstructural trapping sites (grain boundaries, dislocations, phase interfaces), residual stress fields, and micro-porosity. The review demonstrates that FCC-dominated Ni/Co-based and HEA coatings exhibit superior hydrogen resistance due to stable passive films, low hydrogen diffusivity, and efficient trapping. In contrast, Fe-based systems require stringent parameter control to limit martensitic transformation and crack propagation. Current challenges and future directions are outlined, including AI-driven process optimization, in-situ monitoring, functionally graded multimaterial designs, and hydrogen-safe coating development for emerging energy infrastructures. This review provides an integrated framework for designing next-generation laser-clad coatings with optimized performance in corrosive, wear-intensive, and hydrogen-containing environments. © 2026 World Scientific Publishing Company.

Title: The influence of laser energy density on microstructure and wear resistance of TiC-AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy composites coatings
Abstract: AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) coatings incorporating TiC as reinforcement phase are desirable material to improve the wear resistance of the AISI 1045 steel. In this work, 5 wt.% TiC-AlCoCrFeNi coating is successfully prepared via laser cladding, and the influence of laser energy density on microstructure evolution, microhardness as well as wear resistance are systematically investigated. The results show that the main phases of the composite coating are BCC, B2, TiC and M7C3-type carbide. As the laser energy density increases, the free Ti tends to facilitate the formation of solid solutions rather than further synthesizing TiC and M7C3-type carbide in situ due to the strong Marangoni convection and the unique high-entropy effect. The coating exhibits the highest microhardness (990 ± 182 HV0.3) and the most superior wear resistance (2.60 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m)) at a laser energy density of 35 J/mm2. The microhardness slightly decreases while the wear rate significantly increases as the laser energy density increases, which can be attributed to changes in the TiC morphology and strengthening mechanism. At high energy density, the in-situ small-size TiC particles are easily dislodged during the wear process to cause the three-body wear. Moreover, the strengthening mechanism shifts from dislocation, load-bearing and Orowan strengthening (dominated by unmelted TiC and in-situ TiC and M7C3) to solid solution strengthening, which increases brittleness and reduces grain deformation in the wear subsurface, deteriorating the wear resistance. Authors: Yang S.; Ren P.; Ruan W.; Ma J.
Title: Recent advances in the application of high-entropy materials in lithium-based anodes
Abstract: Lithium-ion batteries constitute the cornerstone of modern energy storage. However, commercial graphite anodes are increasingly limited by their theoretical capacity and energy density. Although high-capacity alternatives such as silicon and transition metal oxides have been explored, their practical implementation remains severely bottlenecked by structural instability. High-entropy materials (HEMs) have emerged as promising candidates capable of transcending these conventional limitations. Governed by the four fundamental core effects, HEMs exhibit unique synergistic attributes, including enhanced lattice resilience and superior electrochemical kinetics, that surpass those of conventional binary or ternary counterparts. This review systematically evaluates recent progress in HEM-based anodes for lithium storage, categorizing high-entropy alloys, oxides, and burgeoning derivatives, including sulfides and phosphides. We further dissect the multifaceted storage mechanisms and the practical hurdles facing the predominant high-entropy oxide anodes. Finally, we offer forward-looking perspectives on the field, emphasizing the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) for accelerated material discovery and the pathways toward industrial-scale application. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of State Key Laboratory of Intelligent Construction and Healthy Operation and Maintenance of Deep Underground Engineering, Shenzhen University. Title: Effect of Laser Power on Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of W/HEA/Cu Laser Welded Joints
Abstract: In this study, pure tungsten (W) and pure copper (Cu) blocks were welded using laser beam welding with a high-entropy alloy (HEA) (FeCoNiCrCu) as the intermediate layer. The effects of laser power (1500, 1750, and 2000 W) on the microstructure, hardness, strength, and toughness of the composite welded joints were investigated. Results indicated that under optimized process parameters (1750 W, 2 mm/s), the fusion zone near the Cu side, close to the heat source, exhibited a microstructure with a Cu-rich phase matrix dispersed with irregularly sized round and fine dendritic crystals. Additionally, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cr were uniformly distributed within the Cu matrix, and a fine-grained Cu region was observed at the lower part of the interface near the Cu side. The HEA intermediate layer near the W side exhibited a morphology of elongated and uniform equiaxed grains. At the interface on the W side, NiW and Ni4W phases were formed. The hardness of the joint increased gradually from the Cu side to the W side, and the interaction region between the HEA intermediate layer and the base materials (Cu and W) expanded with increasing laser power. With increasing laser power, the fracture morphology transitioned from equiaxed dimples to elongated dimples and then to a combination of equiaxed and elongated dimples. The shear strength of the W/HEA/Cu laser welded joints initially increased and then decreased, reaching a maximum of 187 MPa at 1750 W. © 2026 American Nuclear Society.

Authors: Wang T.; Chen J.; Tian C.; Chen C.; Park J.H.; Mu W.
Title: Characterization of non-metallic inclusions in Co46Cr30Mn7.5Fe7.5Ni7.5V1.5 dual-phase high entropy alloy with trace amount of Hf addition
Abstract: This study systematically investigates the effect of trace hafnium (Hf) addition (0.069 wt%) on the microstructure evolution and inclusion characteristics in V-alloyed Co-based dual-phase high-entropy alloys. The trace amount of Hf addition was found to mainly form HfOx inclusion in the matrix. This phase replaces the conventional oxide formation and could stabilize the V element in the matrix and against its oxidation. Compare with the Hf-rich HEAs, where Hf segregates at grain boundaries within an FCC-dominant matrix and forms lamellar HCP precipitates. However, Co46Cr30Mn7.5Fe7.5Ni7.5V1.5 with a trace amount of Hf enhances the blocky HCP phase formation and increases the HCP fraction from 15 % to 26 %. Non-metallic inclusion analysis here reveals that V-HEA contains HfOx alongside MnS and HfOx-MnS. In situ observations by high-temperature confocal laser scanning microscopy demonstrate that inclusion motion in the liquid matrix is governed by liquid surface flow and fluctuations. When inter-inclusion distances approach a critical value, attractive capillary force triggers the increase in velocity and acceleration and leads to a rapid collision of inclusions. Smaller inclusions exhibit a weaker attraction and are obviously influenced by the surface flow of liquid. While the larger inclusions are more prone to coarsening through agglomeration. This work provides theoretical and experimental insights into tailoring inclusion characteristics and microstructure evolution in HEAs through trace amounts of critical element addition. © 2025 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Numerical Simulation of Laser Cladding Using Cable Wires
Abstract: Cable wires provide a viable technical pathway for the laser additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the complex interplay of structural and material parameters of cable wires leads to significant variations in molten pool dynamics, which poses challenges to the fabrication of high-quality HEA coatings. To clarify the effects of these key factors on molten pool behavior, a multi-physics numerical model for the laser cladding of Al50Si6Ti8Cr12Cu12Ni12 cable wires was established in this study. A dedicated physical model for cable wires was developed, and the Level Set Method was employed to track fluid interfaces throughout the cladding process. Based on the proposed model, the temperature distribution, stress fields, and elemental homogeneity within the molten pool were systematically investigated. The results reveal that chromium (Cr) addition induces a viscosity reduction, and a torsional pitch of ≤4 mm is critical for achieving defect-free, compositionally uniform HEA coatings, which provides novel insights for process optimization and alloy design of cable-wire laser cladding. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: State-of-the-art review of additive friction stir deposition: microstructural evolution, machine learning applications, and future directions
Source title: Current Opinion in Solid State and Materials Science
Abstract: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is an emergent solid-state additive manufacturing (AM) technique that operates below the melting point temperature of the materials, resulting in lower residual stresses and reduced susceptibility to defects like porosity and hot-cracking compared to fusion-based methods. These benefits position AFSD as a viable alternative to traditional forging for large-scale applications in the aerospace, automotive, marine, and nuclear industries. The interest on AFSD is progressing at a rapid pace and a periodic comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art is of major interest. This comprehensive review presents a detailed summary of key fundamentals, including material flow behaviour and heat generation mechanisms, alongside a critical evaluation of microstructural evolution. Comparative analyses across aluminum, magnesium, titanium, steels, nickel-based superalloys, and high entropy alloys illustrate the diverse grain refinement mechanisms and structural responses that govern the final properties of AFSD-fabricated components. The review places further emphasis on emerging strategies for process modeling and optimization, with particular attention to the integration of machine learning approaches that offer promising insights into real-time defect detection and adaptive process control. The review concludes by addressing the key challenges limiting the industrial translation of AFSD, including surface quality, dimensional accuracy, consistency in multi-material builds, and sustainable material utilization. Perspectives are offered on the development of integrated digital frameworks and real-time monitoring systems. By providing a comprehensive and focused synthesis, this review aims to support the wider adoption of AFSD and foster innovation in solid-state additive manufacturing. It is believed that an advancement of the substantive understanding will expedite the potential industrial implementation of the AFSD technique. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Tribological behavior of nano TiC-reinforced FeCoCrNiMn high entropy alloy composite fabricated by selective laser melting
Abstract: In this study, the microhardness and tribological behavior of high entropy alloy composite (HEAC) reinforced with nano-TiC particles, fabricated using selective laser melting (SLM), were investigated. The HEAC exhibited higher microhardness and superior tribological properties compared to the pure HEA. The microhardness increased from 236 HV to 464 HV, while the friction coefficient (COF) and wear rate decreased to 0.589 and 0.38 × 10−5 mm3/N·m, representing reductions of 8.0% and 41.5%, respectively. The wear mechanism of the pure HEA was predominantly adhesive and oxidative, which was attributed to its low hardness and the delamination of large debris on the worn surface. With the addition of nano-TiC particles, the dominant wear mechanism changed to abrasive and oxidative, accompanied by the formation of a thin tribo-oxide layer. This improvement in wear properties is attributed to the addition of nano-TiC in the HEA matrix, which acts as a lubricant on one hand, and increases the microhardness of the HEAC on the other hand. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Nanoscale oxide-mediated grain-boundary stabilization enables simultaneous strength and ductility in an additively manufactured high-entropy alloy
Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) fabricated by additive manufacturing offer exceptional compositional flexibility; however, controlling grain stability while maintaining high-temperature ductility remains a major challenge. Here, we demonstrate that a minor yttrium (Y) addition (<1000 ppm) markedly modifies the microstructural evolution and tensile behavior of an L12-strengthened HEA produced by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). Compared with the baseline alloy, the Y-bearing HEA retains fine, elongated grains (∼8 μm) after homogenization and controlled cooling, whereas the baseline alloy undergoes severe grain coarsening (∼75 μm). Complementary analysis of (S)TEM, three-dimensional atom-probe (3D-AP) and thermodynamic simulation reveals that this stabilization originates from nanoscale Y-rich oxides formed during solidification and distributed along grain boundaries. The multicomponent high-entropy matrix promotes the enthalpy-driven rejection of Y from grain interiors toward grain boundaries. This behavior originates from severe lattice distortion and atomic-size mismatch, enabling preferential segregation and stable oxide formation. The solid-solid partitioning behavior of FCC matrix and L12 phase remained unchanged with addition of yttrium. Tensile testing from room temperature to 900 °C shows that the Y-bearing HEA exhibits higher strength at room temperature and 650 °C and more than twice the elongation at 750–900 °C without strength loss. Nanoscale Y-rich oxides not only serve as thermally stable grain-growth inhibitors but also suppress stress concentration associated with L21 precipitation through grain-boundary pinning and oxygen scavenging. These findings demonstrate that ppm-level Y microalloying provides an effective grain-boundary engineering strategy for additively manufactured HEAs, offering insights into the design of microstructurally stable alloys with improved high-temperature mechanical performance. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Chen D.; Xie K.; An W.; Ren M.; Cheng Y.; Xia K.; Sun D.; Jia R.; Chen Z.
Title: Enhanced interfacial charge transfer and energy storage of heteroatom-doped porous carbon for solid-state supercapacitors
Abstract: Solid-state supercapacitors (SSCs) are promising energy storage devices due to their high safety, mechanical robustness, fast charge/discharge capability, and ultra-long cycle life. However, their practical application is hindered by relatively low energy densities. In this study, a new strategy is introduced to prepare hierarchical porous carbon materials using chitosan and arginine as precursors, combined with mild H3PO4 doping and activation. When the carbonized chitosan-arginine-H3PO4 (CCA-PX) is applied in three-electrode system of supercapacitors, the optimized CCA-P2 delivers a high specific capacitance of 242.06 F g−1 at a current density of 0.2 A g−1. Meanwhile, the assembled CCA-P2 based symmetric SSCs show an extremely low charge transfer resistance of 0.25 Ω, an outstanding capacity retention of 84.05 % after 10,000 cycles based on KOH gel electrolyte within 1.3 V. Simultaneously, the maximum energy density of 15.4 Wh kg−1 at 225 W kg−1 is achieved based on Na2SO4 gel electrolyte within 1.8 V. Experiments and theoretical calculations have demonstrated that appropriate content of phosphorus doping contributes to optimize the pore structure and surface wettability of the porous carbon materials, thereby improving the charge storage behavior. This work delivers valuable insights for the rational design of high-performance carbon-based electrodes through strategic heteroatom doping. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Revealing mechanisms of dynamic recrystallization during laser directed energy deposition of high-entropy Cantor alloy by multimodal melt pool monitoring
Abstract: Physics-informed grain structure engineering in fusion-based laser additive manufacturing offers great promise for producing high-performance high-entropy alloys, especially for low-cost and compositionally-customized laser directed energy deposition (DED). However, detrimental columnar grains prevalently form in DED due to relatively low solidification rates and extremely high temperature gradients, making them difficult to disrupt and still poorly understood. Here, combining in-situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging and diffraction, thermal imaging, and ex-situ electron microscopy approaches, we reveal a dynamic recrystallization (DRX) mechanism associated with the disruption of epitaxial columnar grains during DED of an exemplary high-entropy Cantor alloy. Multimodal melt pool monitoring enables quantitative analysis of solidification parameters and melt flow characteristics with high temporospatial resolution. Experimental observations combined with thermo-kinetic calculations indicate that both intragranular and intergranular DRX can be activated by localised micro-strains. DRX promotes grain refinement and homogeneity by tailoring energy input with optimally increasing laser power and reducing scan speed, and contributes to a tensile-to-compressive strain reversal during real-time deposition. The results of solidification-dependent grain structure evolution down to melt pool scale provide deeper understanding of in-process grain growth kinetics and enable effective methods for disrupting columnar grain growth during DED processing of novel alloys. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Li Z.; Wang S.; Wang G.; Xiao Z.; Zhang W.; Sun L.; Wang L.; Du M.; Liu M.
Title: Effect of W content on the microstructure, tribological behavior and corrosion resistance of laser-clad TiNbVZr0.5WX refractory high-entropy alloy coatings
Abstract: To address the insufficient surface protection of titanium alloys under wear and corrosion conditions, TiNbVZr0.5Wx (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0) refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) coatings were fabricated on TC4 titanium alloy by laser cladding. The effect of W content on phase constitution, microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, tribological behavior, and corrosion resistance was systematically investigated. The coatings exhibited a typical dendritic/interdendritic structure. With increasing W content, the phase structure evolved from a single BCC solid solution to a multiphase structure consisting of BCC, Zr-rich HCP, and V2Zr Laves phases. Grain refinement was initially achieved, with the W0.5 coating showing the smallest average grain size of 14.37 μm, whereas excessive W led to grain coarsening. The hardness increased continuously with W addition, reaching 794 HV for W1, which corresponds to 2.29 times that of the TC4 substrate. The friction coefficient decreased from 0.39 for W0 to 0.29 for W0.5 and then increased to 0.35 for W1. The improved wear resistance was mainly attributed to grain-refinement strengthening, solid-solution strengthening, and the formation of a compact tribo-oxide film, whereas excessive W promoted brittle Laves-phase-induced delamination wear. The corrosion current density decreased from 1.879 × 10−5 A cm−2 for TC4 to 2.549 × 10−6 A cm−2 for W0.25, owing to the formation of a dense and stable passive film. Considering the combined hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance, the W0.5 coating exhibited the optimal overall performance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Plasma Arc Robot for Direct Wall High-Entropy Alloy Additive Manufacturing
Abstract: Highlights: What are the implications of the main findings? Thin walled AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy was prepared using plasma arc additive manufacturing combined with swing technology to improve forming quality and material density. Systematically study the microstructural evolution and anisotropic mechanical properties, and reveal the mechanism of the influence of sedimentary height on the evolution of FCC/BCC phases. Through the mechanical analysis of AlCoCrFeNi thin-walled high-entropy alloy materials fabricated by plasma arc additive manufacturing, this study examines the practical application prospects of plasma arc manufacturing technology for thin-walled high-entropy alloys and explores its future development directions. Using a plasma arc oscillation process, a 50-layer fine additive experiment was conducted on AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy materials employing both reciprocating and layer-by-layer accumulation methods. The samples were analyzed for overall appearance, microstructure, hardness, and tensile properties. The results indicate that the proportions of columnar and intergranular dendrites in the thin-walled high-entropy alloy specimens are similar, and the columnar dendrites exhibit a uniformly sized cross shape. The variation in Vickers microhardness along the horizontal direction shows lower strength at the edge positions, gradually increasing with horizontal distance. A comparison of the alloy’s transverse and longitudinal tensile specimens revealed that samples parallel to the deposition direction exhibit more regular structural arrangements, while specimens perpendicular to the deposition direction show unavoidable stress concentration at the deposition sites during tensile testing. With the increase in the height of the longitudinal specimens, the FCC structures in the alloy are significantly refined, the organizational arrangement becomes more regular, and the elongation increases. This study elucidates the plasma arc preparation technique for thin-walled high-entropy alloy materials, which is expected to achieve precise control over material composition, accurate observation of grain refinement, and uniform distribution of Vickers hardness, thereby enhancing the mechanical properties and thermal stability of the materials, with promising applications in aerospace, energy, and industrial fields. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Short-range order in face-centered cubic multi-principal element alloys: identification, structure–property relationships, and superfunctional implications
Abstract: Multi-principal element alloys have emerged as an important class of structural materials owing to their exceptional combinations of strength, ductility, and microstructural stability. Increasing evidence suggests that chemical short-range ordering plays a critical role in governing these properties by modifying local bonding, defect energetics, and deformation pathways. Yet, a coherent understanding of short-range order in face-centered cubic multi-principal element alloys remains elusive, not only because its formation and manifestation are highly sensitive to alloy chemistry and thermal history, but also because fundamental questions remain unresolved regarding how short-range order should be defined, measured, and interpreted in chemically complex solid solutions. In particular, the rigorous distinction of short-range ordering from clustering, deformation-induced local ordering, long-range ordered precipitates, and diffraction-related artifacts remains a central challenge in the field. In this review, we critically examine the current understanding of short-range order in face-centered cubic multi-principal element alloys, with emphasis on its thermodynamic origin, thermal evolution, quantitative descriptors, and multiscale characterization. A distinctive contribution of this review is the proposal of a practical correlative protocol for identifying “true short-range order”, with emphasis on the minimum evidence required to distinguish genuine short-range order from clustering, long-range ordered precipitates, and measurement-related artifacts. Particular attention is devoted to recent advances in atomistic modeling, atom probe tomography, and transmission electron microscopy-based approaches, which have expanded access to local chemical ordering while also exposing important methodological limitations. We further assess how short-range order perturbs defect energetics, dislocation behavior, stacking-fault-mediated deformation, strengthening, and other kinetic processes across multiple length scales. By integrating recent advances with current controversies, this review seeks to clarify the conditions under which short-range ordering can be identified rigorously, linked defensibly to measurable properties, and ultimately used as a tunable microstructural design parameter in high-performance and superfunctional high-entropy materials. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Progress in Laser Surface Modification of Magnesium Alloys (Invited); [镁 合 金 激 光 表 面 改 性 技 术 进 展（特 邀）]
Abstract: Significance Magnesium (Mg) alloys, valued for their high specific strength, low density, and biocompatibility, are promising materials for lightweight structures and biomedical implants. However, their poor corrosion and wear resistance limits wider application. Conventional surface treatments—such as anodic oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, and micro-arc oxidation—often produce porous, weakly adherent coatings prone to failure under complex stress. Laser surface modification (LSM) offers a superior alternative with precise control, minimal thermal damage, and compatibility with complex geometries. Through rapid heating and cooling, LSM refines microstructures and promotes beneficial phase transformations, enhancing surface performance without compromising the substrate. Mg alloys serve crucial roles in aerospace, automotive, and biomedical fields, and their improved surface durability directly determines their service reliability and lifespan. Furthermore, the adaptability of laser surface modification to both structural applications and bio-degradable implants expands its relevance across multiple research frontiers—from surface engineering to biomaterials science. Current LSM techniques include laser surface melting, cladding, shock peening, and texturing, which can be classified into three mechanisms—rapid melting, impact strengthening, and micro/nano modification. This review summarizes recent advances, mechanisms, and challenges in these approaches and outlines future directions to guide the continued development and practical application of laser-modified Mg alloys. Progress The influence mechanism of laser surface modification on Mg alloys can be categorized into three dominant approaches: rapid melting and solidification, shock-induced strengthening, and micro-nano structural modification. Each mechanism has different effects. 1) Rapid melting and solidification Laser surface remelting (LSR) and laser cladding (LC) form the core of rapid solidification strategies. Through extreme heating-cooling cycles, these processes refine grain structures, dissolve harmful secondary phases, and homogenize solute distributions, leading to dense protective layers and superior corrosion resistance. In the study of laser surface remelting of AZ41 alloy, after laser treatment, a heterogeneous remelting layer of over 220 μm is achieved in the coarse-grained alloy. Compared with the untreated original sample, the hardness of the remelted layer surface is 1.62 times higher, the low cycle fatigue life is 2.3 times higher, and the high cycle fatigue life is 18.6 times higher. Similarly, laser surface remelting synergistically strengthens the Mg-9Li-Al alloy, as Al redistribution and fine precipitate formation contribute to a hardness improvement up to 168 HV and enhanced corrosion resistance. Laser cladding further extends the modification potential by incorporating metallic, ceramic, or high-entropy alloy systems as reinforcement coatings. In composite systems, the combination of Al-Ti-TiC-CNTs and Al-TiC-B4C structures achieves remarkable microhardness (>290 HV) and a two-order reduction in corrosion current density, indicating synergistic strengthening by dispersed reinforcement and refined matrix. Moreover, recent developments in medium- and high-entropy alloy coatings have yielded coatings with hardness up to 10‒12 times that of the substrate, offering both superior wear resistance and corrosion stability. Overall, laser cladding is evolving toward multi-elemental and entropy-stabilized designs, combining metallurgical bonding with tunable surface functionality. 2) Shock-induced strengthening Laser shock peening (LSP) employs high-energy shock waves to induce surface nano crystallization and compressive residual stress, improving fatigue life, hardness, and corrosion resistance. Under the action of LSP, gradient microstructure will be formed: dense dislocation entanglement, twins and nanocrystals form a layered strengthening region extending hundreds of microns under the surface. These gradient structures can restrain crack initiation and improve strength and ductility at the same time. When integrated with auxiliary techniques such as electro pulsing, LSP yields deeper residual stress fields and further grain refinement, optimizing stress corrosion cracking resistance. Biomedical applications particularly benefit from this non-thermal process—LSP-treated Mg alloys show up to 56.2% reduction in corrosion rate and enhanced biocompatibility by modulating degradation behavior. This indicates strong potential for controlled biodegradation in implantable Mg systems. 3) Micro-nano structural modification Laser surface texturing (LST) enables precise construction of micro-nano architectures such as grooves, ripples, and pits, which tailor surface wettability, friction behavior, and biological response. In medical Mg alloys, textures such as flower-like or honeycomb microstructures markedly improve corrosion resistance and tribological behavior. For instance, laser-fabricated textures on WE43 and RZ5 alloys reduce corrosion current densities by an order of magnitude compared with untreated samples. In addition, different texture geometries can affect the proliferation of osteoblasts; microgrooves promote cellular alignment, while submicron ripples enhance cell adhesion and differentiation. Beyond biomedical uses, LST also facilitates functional surface design for self-healing, anti-biofouling, and superhydrophobic coatings. Techniques combining femtosecond laser structuring with chemical modification yield switchable superhydrophobic/ lubricating surfaces, offering corrosion potentials up to − 1.388 V and over 10-fold improvement in charge transfer resistance. Furthermore, LST acts as an effective pretreatment for coating adhesion; laser-induced roughness and interlocking structures greatly improve the bonding strength of phosphate, micro-arc oxidation, hydroxyapatite, and polymer coatings. This synergy enables long-term protection (>100 h immersion stability) and reliable performance for Mg-based composites and implants. Conclusions and Prospects Laser surface modification of magnesium alloys represents a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field integrating materials science, surface physics, and laser processing. The key conclusions drawn from recent progress include: 1) Rapid melting and solidification enable the formation of refined microstructures and metallurgically bonded coatings, significantly enhancing hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance. 2) Shock-induced strengthening introduces beneficial residual stress and nano crystallization without altering chemical composition, achieving a balance between mechanical robustness and corrosion protection, particularly relevant for biodegradable systems. 3) Micro-nano structural modification provides a flexible pathway to regulate interfacial behavior and multifunctionality, achieving synergistic improvements in corrosion resistance, wear performance, and biocompatibility. Looking forward, several promising directions emerge: 1) Integration of ultrafast laser and beam-shaping techniques to achieve multi-scale hybrid textures for precise control of interface reactivity and wettability. 2) Development of multi-energy-field hybrid processing, coupling laser treatment with cold spraying, micro-arc oxidation, or electrochemical deposition for coatings with superior adhesion, long-term protection, and self-healing capabilities. 3) Intelligent optimization via machine learning, establishing databases linking process parameters, microstructure, and performance to enable real-time control and predictive design. 4) In-situ monitoring and closed-loop feedback for laser processes, combining optical, acoustic, and thermal sensing to ensure process stability and reproducibility. With continuous advances in ultrafast lasers, materials design, and data-driven process control, laser surface modification is poised to deliver comprehensive and durable enhancements in Mg alloy performance. Its integration into aerospace, transportation, and biomedical manufacturing will provide robust pathways for lightweight, corrosion-resistant, and biocompatible systems, marking a major leap toward sustainable, high-performance material engineering. © 2026 Chinese Laser Press. Authors: Li H.; Yuan Y.; Xu X.
Title: Microstructure evolution and dual-phase transformation during deep undercooling by rapid solidification of CrFeNi equiatomic medium entropy alloy
Abstract: This study investigates the rapid solidification behavior of an equiatomic CrFeNi medium-entropy alloy under deep undercooling conditions and reveals significant grain refinement in the solidified microstructure. Glass fluxing purification combined with cyclic superheating was employed to achieve deep undercooling and rapid solidification of the CrFeNi alloy. The crystallization process during rapid solidification was recorded using a high-speed camera, which captured two recalescence events. The solidification velocity was found to generally increase with increasing undercooling. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis was conducted to examine the grain orientation and misorientation distribution. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) analysis of a sample with a maximum undercooling of 270 K revealed the presence of precipitates within the microstructure, including high-density stacking faults, nanotwins, and nanoscale phases. A large number of Cr-rich phases were observed to precipitate from the FCC matrix, while the Fe and Ni contents in these phases were minimal. Vickers microhardness testing was performed to study the variation in microhardness with increasing undercooling. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Lei Z.; Du L.; Zhang M.; Yang L.; Wada T.; Jiang J.; Han J.; Lu Z.; Kato H.
Title: Entropy-regulated nanocrystallization in PdPt-based metallic glasses for dual-phase HER catalysts
Abstract: Hydrogen, characterized by the high energy density and environmental friendliness, is considered an ideal energy carrier. As a common method for hydrogen production, the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER) benefits significantly from the selection of efficient catalysts to enhance overall efficiency. High-entropy metal glasses (HEMGs), possessing multi-component synergistic effects and long-range disordered atomic structures, represent a class of highly efficient catalysts. In this study, three amorphous alloys with distinct mixing entropies were designed: PdPtCuNiP, PdNiCuP, and PtNiCuP. By leveraging the atomic sluggish diffusion effect inherent in high-entropy alloys to overcome the challenge of uncontrollable crystallization rates, the PdPtCuNiP amorphous/nanocrystalline composite material was successfully synthesized. The composite combines the intrinsically high electrochemical activity of the amorphous matrix with the galvanic cell effect induced by nanocrystals. Furthermore, dealloying was formed through potentiostatic corrosion, which further improved the HER catalytic performance. In 0.5 M H2SO4 solution, the catalyst achieved an overpotential of only 32 mV at a current density of 10 mA/cm2, surpassing the performance of most available electrocatalysts. © 2026

Authors: Qiu H.; Guo Y.; Lu B.; Zhu J.; Wu L.; Yue Y.; Wang Y.; Yan X.
Title: Effect of Mo content on solidification and microstructural evolution of laser cladded FeCoCrNiMox high-entropy alloys
Abstract: The effect of Mo content on phase stability, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response of laser cladded FeCoCrNiMox high-entropy alloys was systematically investigated. With increasing Mo content, pronounced changes in solidification behavior and microstructural architecture were observed under rapid, non-equilibrium conditions. The Mo-free FeCoCrNi alloy exhibits a stable FCC structure and coarse columnar grains with an average grain size of approximately 96 μm, indicating relatively stable directional solidification. Moderate Mo addition leads to significant grain refinement and altered solidification morphology. FeCoCrNiMo10 develops a mixed columnar–equiaxed microstructure with equiaxed grains of about 2 μm, while maintaining FCC phase stability. Further increasing Mo content results in extensive equiaxed grains with characteristic sizes of 8–16 μm, accompanied by pronounced Mo segregation and the formation of σ and Laves phases. The emergence of these intermetallic phases is associated with strong local strain localization and incoherent or semi-coherent σ/FCC interfaces, as revealed by EBSD and TEM analyses. The microstructural evolution induced by Mo addition is reflected in the macroscopic mechanical response. Vickers microhardness increases markedly from 150 HV0.2 in FeCoCrNi to 339 HV0.2 in FeCoCrNiMo10 and further to 691 HV0.2 in FeCoCrNiMo20. However, while excessive Mo addition maximizes hardness, it also leads to increased microstructural heterogeneity and reduced fracture resistance. In contrast, FeCoCrNiMo10 achieves a favorable balance between strengthening and structural integrity. Overall, the results demonstrate that Mo content defines a compositional stability window for FCC-based FeCoCrNi alloys processed under rapid solidification conditions. These findings provide insight into the compositional design of refractory-element-containing high-entropy alloys, highlighting the importance of balancing grain refinement, phase stability, and structural integrity. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Tailoring microstructure, mechanical and magnetic properties of additively manufactured AlCoCuFeNi alloy via process control and heat treatment
Abstract: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation structural and functional applications because of their excellent mechanical performance, thermal stability, and magnetic properties. In this work, equiatomic AlCoCuFeNi was successfully fabricated using Laser Engineered Net Shaping Directed Energy Deposition (LENS-DED), and the influence of post-deposition heat treatment on its microstructural evolution, mechanical behavior, and magnetic performance was systematically investigated. Process optimization enabled the fabrication of near fully dense components with a relative density of 99.89% as confirmed by high-resolution computed tomography (CT) analysis. The as-printed alloy exhibited a heterogeneous dual-phase microstructure consisting of BCC (B2/A2) and Cu-rich FCC (L12/FCC) phases. Heat treatment, designed using differential scanning calorimetry and CALPHAD thermodynamic predictions, promoted phase redistribution, grain growth, and secondary phase evolution, resulting in significant changes in both mechanical and magnetic responses. The evolved microstructure exhibited a fracture strength of 1.921 GPa, yield strength of 946 MPa, ductility of 27.46%, and microhardness of 368 HV. Magnetic measurements revealed excellent soft magnetic behavior with a saturation magnetization of 85.18 emu/g, a low coercivity of 3.34 Oe, and a Curie temperature of approximately 792 °C. The improved mechanical performance is attributed to the combined effects of heterogeneous dual-phase strengthening and heat-treatment-induced phase evolution, while the magnetic response is governed by changes in phase constitution and grain structure. These findings establish processing-microstructure-property relationships for additively manufactured AlCoCuFeNi and demonstrate its potential as a multifunctional alloy for advanced structural and magnetic applications. © 2026 .

Title: Frontiers of Direct Energy Deposition: Process Innovation and Intelligent Regulation; [直接能量沉积技术前沿：工艺创新和智能调控]
Abstract: A systematic review of the latest research advances in DED technology was provided, focusing on four key developmental directions: multi-heat source hybridization, material supply innovation, energy field regulation, and AI-driven processes. Regarding multi-heat source hybridization, combined processes, such as laser-arc hybridization, the complementary mechanism between different heat sources were leveraged, effectively balancing processing efficiency and forming accuracy. Regarding material supply innovation, novel feeding approaches, including twisted wire, multi-wire, and wire-powder synergistic feeding, had significantly expanded the capability to fabricate functional gradient materials and multi-principal element alloys. It laid the material foundation for enhancing the performance of components overall. Regarding energy field regulation, several methods such as pulse modulation, path planning, and multi-physical field coupling achieved precise control over molten pool dynamics and microstructural evolution. Regarding AI driving, the integration of machine learning and other data-driven techniques expedited the intelligent evolution of DED technology in areas such as processing parameter optimization, intelligent defect diagnosis, and digital twin system development. © 2026, Chinese Academy of Space Technology. Authors: Luo Y.; Yu Y.; Ren P.; Zhan S.; Chen Y.; Yuan Z.; Tang H.; Qiao Z.
Title: Research Progress on Corrosion and Wear Behavior of High￣Entropy Alloys in Marine Environments; [海洋环境下高熵合金的腐蚀与磨损行为研究进展]
Abstract: Marine equipment and offshore engineering components are inevitably exposed to harsh service environments characterized by high chloride concentrations, dissolved oxygen gradients, temperature fluctuations, and continuous or intermittent mechanical loads. Under such complex conditions, material degradation is rarely governed by pure corrosion or wear alone; instead, tribocorrosion, the corrosion - wear synergism, dominates the damage evolution, leading to accelerated material loss and premature failure. Traditional structural alloys often exhibit limited resistance to this coupled degradation due to insufficient passive film stability, inadequate hardness, or poor microstructural adaptability. In recent years, high - entropy alloys (HEAs), composed of multiple principal elements in near - or equiatomic ratios, have attracted increasing attention. Their distinctive features, including severe lattice distortion, high configurational entropy, compositional tunability, and diverse strengthening mechanisms, provide a new approach to regulating the interaction between electrochemical corrosion and mechanical wear. In chloride - containing environments, such as 3.5% (mass fraction) NaCl solution and artificial seawater, some progress has been made in the research on the tribocorrosion behavior of HEAs. From a compositional perspective, key alloying elements such as Cr, Mo, Ti, and Al play different roles in passivation, tribofilm formation, and mechanical strengthening. HEAs containing Cr and Mo usually exhibit excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense and stable passive films formed, while Ti and Al can form oxide - rich tribofilms, which improve load - bearing capacity and reduce direct metal contact during sliding. From a microstructural viewpoint, single - phase FCC or BCC solid solutions, dual - phase structures, and precipitation - strengthened HEAs show markedly different tribocorrosion responses. Grain refinement, solid solution strengthening, and the introduction of nanoscale precipitates can inhibit plastic deformation, reduce wear - induced damage, and alleviate passive film rupture. In addition, fabrication and surface engineering technologies, such as additive manufacturing and laser cladding, can regulate the microstructure, defect density, residual stress, and interfacial bonding of HEAs, thereby significantly affecting their tribocorrosion performance. In terms of testing methodologies, electrochemical - tribological coupling techniques, including open - circuit potential monitoring during sliding, potentiodynamic polarization under applied load, and material loss partitioning based on ASTM G119, are widely used to quantitatively evaluate the synergistic effect of corrosion and wear. Mechanistically, the tribocorrosion behavior of HEAs in marine environments is governed by the dynamic competition among passive film formation, mechanical damage, and repassivation. Mechanical actions such as sliding, fretting, or abrasion continuously damage the passive films and expose fresh metal surfaces, which accelerates anodic dissolution. In contrast, the chemical complexity and elemental synergy of HEAs can enhance repassivation kinetics and shorten the time window of active dissolution. Depending on alloy composition and microstructural stability, different synergistic regimes may dominate. For HEAs with relatively weak passivation or low hardness, wear - accelerated corrosion dominates, and micro - cutting and ploughing accelerate chloride ion penetration and localized corrosion. In contrast, HEAs with robust passive films, high hardness, and stable tribofilms exhibit corrosion - inhibited wear. Oxide tribolayers and compact wear debris reduce friction and material loss. Despite considerable progress, there are still several challenges, including the high sensitivity of tribocorrosion behavior to testing parameters, incomplete understanding of microstructural evolution and electrochemical responses under dynamic loading, and the lack of long - term performance data under real marine conditions. Future research should focus on mechanism - based alloy design, integrate passivation chemistry, mechanical strength, and microstructural stability, and combine advanced in situ characterization and multiscale modeling. Overall, high - entropy alloys show significant potential in mitigating tribocorrosion synergistic degradation in marine environments. Continuous optimization of composition, regulation of microstructure, and innovation of processes are expected to promote the development of next - generation marine materials with higher durability and reliability. © 2026 China Academy of Machinery Wuhan Research Institute of Materials Protection Co., Ltd. Authors: Li D.; Liu H.; Wang W.; Chen P.; Hao J.; Yang H.; He X.; Yu G.
Title: Construct laminated heterogeneous structures to enhance mechanical properties of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy coatings by in-situ deformation assisted laser cladding activating dynamic recrystallization
Abstract: Compared with additive manufacturing, laser cladding involves lower thermal accumulation and a faster cooling rate of the molten pool, the single plastic deformation experienced by each coating track makes it difficult for dynamic recrystallization to be activated solely by the processing energy. In this study, a CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating with a laminated heterogeneous structure was synchronously fabricated via in-situ thermal rolling assisted laser cladding process. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that higher temperatures increased strain, promoting the formation of Shockley partial dislocations and stacking faults. Dislocation interactions generated Hirth locks, which hindered dislocation motion and improved plastic deformation resistance. Experimental results showed that the plastic flow induced by thermal field assisted in-situ rolling significantly reduced the porosity and surface roughness of the coating. The application of the thermal field resulted in the formation of a severely plastically deformed band oriented at approximately 45°, within which recrystallization occurred, leading to the formation of fine-grained regions, recrystallization was not observed in the surrounded areas. A laminated heterogeneous structure with alternating coarse and fine grains was formed inside the coating, and the partial recrystallization that occurred during fabrication contributed to the development of this internal heterogeneity. The introduction of the thermal field caused a transition in the recrystallization mechanism within the severely deformed zone, from static recrystallization to dynamic recrystallization. The combined effects of reduced porosity, increased microhardness, and heterogeneous structure strengthening enhanced the mechanical properties of the coating. The microhardness was significantly increased from 214.6HV0.3 to 284.3HV0.3. This study presents a novel approach for designing heterogeneous HEA coatings and clarifies the microstructural evolution mechanisms during fabrication. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Role of nickel in tensile response and fracture of as-cast Al–5Cu-1.2Fe alloys: Intermetallic evolution analyzed by X-ray computed microtomography
Source title: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
Abstract: The presence of Fe-rich intermetallic compounds (IMCs) in recycled Al alloys often leads to coarse, brittle morphologies that degrade mechanical performance. Ni additions have been proposed to alter the formation and morphology of these phases, but their effects on tensile behavior and fracture mechanisms in Al–Cu–Fe alloys remain unclear, while three-dimensional (3D) characterization of IMCs is limited. This work investigates the influence of 1 wt% Ni on the solidification, microstructure, tensile properties, and fracture behavior of directionally solidified Al–5Cu–1.2Fe alloys. Al13Fe4 phase was identified in the ternary alloy, whereas Al9FeNi formed in the Ni-containing alloy. At high cooling rates (∼13.0 oC/s), the ternary alloy exhibited higher tensile strength (>265 MPa) and elongation (>15 %) than the quaternary alloy (∼230 MPa, ∼9 %). Although Ni addition reduced the room-temperature properties compared with the ternary alloy, they remain high relative to conventional as-cast commercial Al–Cu based alloys, with the Al9FeNi phase expected to provide benefits for thermal stability. Micro-CT revealed bulky, branched 3D Al13Fe4 networks in the ternary alloy, whereas Al9FeNi particles in the quaternary alloy were partially refined but retained branched morphologies aligned with the solidification direction. Particle size distributions confirmed larger IMCs in the ternary alloy and more refined particles in the Ni-containing alloy at higher cooling rates, although coarse particles persisted at lower rates. Surface area-to-volume ratios were consistently higher in the ternary alloy, indicating more efficient stress transfer during loading compared to the quaternary alloy. © 2025 The Authors.

Authors: Tian Y.; Lu D.; Cui X.; Wang W.; Lu Y.
Title: Corrosion resistance of laser additive manufactured high-entropy alloys after cyclic deep cryogenic treatment
Abstract: The accumulation of significant residual stresses within the laser additive manufacturing (LAM) components may significantly affect the corrosion resistance. In this study, we investigated the effect of the cyclic deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) on the corrosion resistance of LAM CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization tests. In comparison to the as-built sample, the DCT10 sample exhibits an elevated corrosion potential and a reduced corrosion current density, specifically −0.295 V vs. SCE and 0.039 μA cm−2, respectively. After the DCT process, a more stable passive film leads to significant enhancement in corrosion resistance. This is attributed to the high compressive residual stress (∼−331 MPa) and dense dislocations (∼0.54 × 1014 m−2) of the DCT10 sample promotes the formation of dense passive film, which effectively mitigates local corrosion and enhances corrosion resistance of the samples. This work presents an effective and non-destructive method to enhance the corrosion resistance of LAM CrMnFeCoNi HEAs, providing significant insights for elevating the application potential of LAM alloys. © 2025 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Niu P.; Li R.; Ji W.; Gan K.; Yuan T.; Li Z.; Zhou K.
Title: Synergy of stacking fault energy and lattice friction on dislocation-mediated strengthening and fatigue resistance in additively manufactured FCC high-entropy alloy
Abstract: Complicated dislocation configurations generated in supersaturated solid solutions of laser-based additively manufactured (AM) alloys are motivated by the competition between intrinsic factors, including stacking fault energy (SFE) and lattice frication stress (LFS). However, the synergistic effects of SFE and LFS, which control the dislocation arrays and slip mode, accordingly govern the mechanical response of AM single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) alloys, remain unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate the roles of SFE and LFS in dictating mechanical properties by examining dislocation configuration evolution in model materials of single-phase Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0 ∼ 0.3) high entropy alloys (HEAs) produced by a conventional laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) approach. Through tuning the Al content of these alloys, the SFE and LFS values can be modified to gain different dislocation configurations in the FCC-structured matrix. Microstructural characterization, along with quantitative analysis via atomic simulation, reveals that reduced SFE combined with elevated LFS yields a pronounced transition of dislocation configuration from cell structures toward planar-slip arrays. This markedly tunes the dislocation-mediated behaviors upon deformation, and accordingly enhances the strength-ductility synergy, i.e., the yield strength increases from 485 MPa ( x =0) to 729 MPa ( x =0.3) while maintaining a large uniform elongation (25%). High-cycle fatigue analysis further demonstrated that reduced SFE promotes planar dislocation arrays, increases dislocation density, and facilitates deformation twinning and stacking faulting during cyclic loading, thereby amplifying the dynamic Hall-Petch effect and inhibiting crack initiation and growth. Notably, localized dynamic recrystallization occurs near cracks in the low-SFE model alloy, reducing dislocation density and dissipating accumulated fatigue-induced stress. This study reveals the origins of dislocation configuration determined by the competition between SFE and LFS, and demonstrates the dislocation-mediated mechanisms controlled by this competition, which improves the strength-ductility synergy and fatigue resistance of AM-produced alloys, thereby shedding light on the design of high-performance structural materials. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: From entropy stabilization to σ-phase engineering: A multiscale review of ordering, deformation, surface degradation, and atomistic modelling in Mo-modified Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys
Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have evolved beyond the concept of entropy-stabilized solid solutions to become compositionally complex materials whose properties are governed by the interplay among thermodynamics, diffusion kinetics, chemical ordering, phase transformations, and processing history. Among these systems, Mo-modified Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs have attracted considerable attention because of their excellent mechanical properties, thermal stability, corrosion resistance, oxidation resistance, and wear performance. This review critically examines the transition from entropy stabilization to σ-phase engineering, highlighting the roles of local chemical ordering, elemental partitioning, lattice distortion, diffusion-controlled precipitation, and microstructural evolution in governing phase stability and alloy performance. Particular emphasis is placed on the dual role of the σ phase, demonstrating that finely dispersed precipitates can enhance strength, creep resistance, wear resistance, and thermal stability. In contrast, excessive or interconnected σ-phase networks promote embrittlement and environmental degradation. Recent advances in corrosion, oxidation, tribology, additive manufacturing, rapid solidification, spark plasma sintering, and laser processing are reviewed, together with emerging computational approaches including CALPHAD, density functional theory, molecular dynamics, Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME), and machine learning. The review also discusses industrial scalability, manufacturing challenges, and the economic implications of Mo addition, emphasizing that future alloy design should optimize rather than maximize Mo content to achieve the best balance between performance, manufacturability, and cost. By integrating processing–microstructure–property–degradation relationships within a unified framework, this review provides design guidelines and identifies future research directions for the development and commercialization of next-generation Mo-modified Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs for demanding high-temperature and corrosive environments. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Interfacial Microstructure Evolution and Mechanical Properties in Laser Welded AZ31/5A06 Dissimilar Joints with In-situ AlCrTiV Multi-principal Element Alloy Interlayer
Abstract: During the laser welding of Mg/Al dissimilar alloys, the existence of brittle Mg–Al intermetallic compounds (IMCs) at the joint interface has been identified as the main factor affecting the mechanical properties of welded joints. Multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs) are excellent interlayer materials. However, their high cost and limited variety restrict their applications as interlayer materials. This study employed elementally blended powders of Ti, V, and Cr to execute laser welding trials on the lap joints of Mg/Al dissimilar alloys within situ-synthesized MPEA as the interlayer. The effects of different laser powers and welding speeds on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the lap joints were analyzed, and the interfacial metallurgical products were calculated and discussed. Our results indicate that molten Ti, V, and Cr successfully underwent a metallurgical reaction with Al derived from the melted aluminum alloy parent material under optimal laser welding parameters, leading to the in-situ formation of the AlCrTiV phase. When the interlayer of the specimens is composed of the AlCrTiV phase, it acts as a barrier to significantly impede the extensive diffusion of Mg and effectively curtail the formation of Mg–Al IMCs, thereby improving the shear performance of the joints. The specimen with a welding parameter of 1155 W and 35 mm/s achieved a maximum tensile-shear load of 1122.56 N. Compared with the joints devoid of the MPEA phase, there was a notable enhancement in tensile properties by 56.41%, accompanied by a substantial increase in elongation of 57.73%. Title: Crack defects and formation mechanism of multi-principal element alloy FeCr0.5NiCu0.5 coating fabricated by Laser cladding
Abstract: Laser cladding technology presents a promising method for fabricating multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) coatings, yet cracks remain one of the most prevalent defects in HEA laser cladding. In this study, FeCr0.5NiCu0.5 multi-principal element alloy coatings were produced on heat-resistant steel (12Cr1MoV) using laser cladding with varying scanning speeds. The study systematically examined the types and mechanisms of cracks within the multi-principal element alloy coatings and also summarized the effects of scanning speed on the coating's dilution rate and cooling rate. Results indicate that an increase in scanning speed significantly elevates the coating's dilution rate and the risk of cracking. With the increase in scanning speed, the cooling rate has risen from 2.68 × 103 K/s to 3.7 × 104 K/s, achieving an order of magnitude improvement. The secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) has diminished from 4.02 µm to 1.8 µm, resulting in a significant refinement of the grains. Cracks within the coating are categorized into macrocracks and microcracks. Macrocracks originate at the interface between the coating and the substrate, induced by the substantial thermal expansion coefficient mismatch between the multi-principal element alloy and heat-resistant steel. Microcracks manifest as intergranular cracks due to the distribution of low-melting-point Cu elements along the grain boundaries, which increases the brittleness of the boundaries. © The Author(s) 2026
